g1.subject: Accounts – AS 23
g1.title: Associates in consolidated accounts
g1.body:
• Associate: an enterprise in which the investor has significant influence, and which is neither a subsidiary nor a joint venture.
• Holding 20% or more of the voting power (directly, or through subsidiaries) is presumed to give significant influence, unless clearly shown otherwise.
• In consolidated financial statements, an associate is accounted for using the equity method.
• Equity method: start at cost (goodwill or capital reserve identified at acquisition is part of the carrying amount); add the investor's share of profit; deduct dividends received.
• If losses reduce the carrying amount to nil, further losses are generally not recognised.
• Equity method is NOT used if the investment is held exclusively for disposal in the near future, or the associate works under severe long-term restrictions on transferring funds – then AS 13 applies.

g2.subject: FM – Cost of capital
g2.title: CAPM in one card
g2.body:
Ke = Rf + β × (Rm − Rf)
Rf = risk-free rate, β = beta, Rm = market return, (Rm − Rf) = market risk premium

Example: Rf 7%, Rm 13%, β 1.5
Ke = 7% + 1.5 × (13% − 7%) = 7% + 9% = 16%

β = 1 → as risky as the market; β > 1 → riskier; β < 1 → less risky.
For a new project with a different risk, use the PROJECT's beta, not the company's beta.
Common mistake: β × Rm instead of β × (Rm − Rf).
g2.link: Linked to today's case MCQ: CAPM – Project-specific Ke

g1.subject: GST – Sec 2(30) & 2(74)
g1.title: Composite supply vs Mixed supply
g1.body:
Composite supply → items NATURALLY bundled and supplied together in the ordinary course of business. Mixed supply → items NOT naturally bundled, but sold together for one price.

Composite: one item is the principal supply. Mixed: no principal supply.

Composite: taxed at the rate of the principal supply. Mixed: taxed at the HIGHEST rate among the items.

Example – Composite: goods sent with packing, transport and insurance. Mixed: a Diwali gift box with sweets, chocolates, dry fruits and a soft drink.

Quick check: 'Would a customer normally expect these together?' Yes → composite. No → mixed.
g1.link: Linked to today's general MCQ: Sec 8 – Mixed supply

g2.subject: Costing – Material cost
g2.title: EOQ in one card
g2.body:
EOQ = √(2 × A × O ÷ C)
A = annual demand (units), O = cost per order, C = carrying cost per unit per year

Example: A 10,000 units, O ₹100, C ₹2
EOQ = √(2 × 10,000 × 100 ÷ 2) = √10,00,000 = 1,000 units
Orders per year = 10,000 ÷ 1,000 = 10
Ordering cost = 10 × 100 = ₹1,000; Carrying cost = 1,000 ÷ 2 × 2 = ₹1,000

At EOQ, ordering cost = carrying cost.
If C is given as a % of price, C = price × %.
Demand 4 times → EOQ only 2 times (square root!).

g1.subject: Accounts – AS 2
g1.title: GST in the cost of inventory?
g1.body:
❌ Raw material bought at ₹118 (₹100 + ₹18 GST). Full input tax credit is available, but the store values the stock at ₹118.

✅ Correct: cost of purchase EXCLUDES taxes that are later recoverable from the tax authorities. Stock is valued at ₹100.

Cost of purchase INCLUDES: purchase price, import duties, non-recoverable taxes, freight inwards, handling and other costs directly linked to buying.
DEDUCT: trade discounts and rebates.
If ITC is NOT available, the GST becomes part of the cost.

g2.subject: SM – Strategic intent
g2.title: Vision vs Mission vs Goals vs Objectives
g2.body:
Vision → WHERE the organisation wants to be in the long-term future (an inspiring picture).
Mission → WHY it exists and WHAT it does now – its purpose and business.
Goals → BROAD, open-ended outcomes it wants to achieve.
Objectives → SPECIFIC, measurable and time-bound targets that turn goals into action.

Example: Vision – 'most trusted healthcare innovator by 2045'. Goal – 'strengthen global presence'. Objective – 'enter 5 new countries and earn 20% of revenue from exports by 2028'.

Trick: Vision dreams, Mission explains, Goals point the way, Objectives count.
g2.link: Linked to today's case MCQ: Vision, Goals, Objectives

g1.subject: Accounts – AS 4
g1.title: Events after the Balance Sheet date
g1.body:
• Adjusting events: give more evidence about conditions that EXISTED on the B/S date → adjust the accounts. (Debtor already weak declared insolvent; court case decided.)
• Non-adjusting events: NEW conditions after the B/S date → don't adjust; disclose if material. (Fire, flood, share issue.)
• Going concern: if events show the business is no longer a going concern, the accounts are NOT prepared on going-concern basis – even though it is a later event.
• Proposed dividend after the B/S date: not a liability on the B/S date – disclose in notes.
• Period covered: B/S date to the date the Board approves the accounts.
g1.link: Linked to today's general MCQ: AS 4 – Events after the B/S date

g2.subject: SM – Porter's five forces
g2.title: The 5 forces: 'Rahul Never Skips Big Snacks'
g2.body:
R – Rivalry among existing competitors (the centre of the model)
N – New entrants (threat of entry)
S – Substitutes (threat of substitute products)
B – Buyers (bargaining power of buyers)
S – Suppliers (bargaining power of suppliers)

The stronger the forces, the lower the industry's profit potential.
Government is NOT a sixth force – it works through these five (e.g. licences raise entry barriers).

g1.subject: Law – Sec 96
g1.title: AGM: all the time limits
g1.body:
• First AGM: within 9 months from the close of the FIRST financial year. No other AGM is needed in the year of incorporation.
• Later AGMs: within 6 months from the close of the financial year.
• Gap between two AGMs: not more than 15 months.
• Extension by ROC: up to 3 months for special reasons – NOT for the first AGM.
• Time and place: business hours (9 AM–6 PM), on a day that is not a national holiday, at the registered office or in the same city, town or village.
• One Person Company: AGM provisions do not apply.
g1.link: Linked to today's case MCQ: Sec 96 – AGM timeline

g2.subject: Costing – Employee cost
g2.title: Halsey vs Rowan in one card
g2.body:
Halsey bonus = 50% × Time saved × Rate per hour
Rowan bonus = (Time saved ÷ Time allowed) × Time taken × Rate per hour

Example: Time allowed 10 hrs, time taken 8 hrs, rate ₹50/hr
Halsey = 50% × 2 × 50 = ₹50 → earnings ₹450
Rowan = (2 ÷ 10) × 8 × 50 = ₹80 → earnings ₹480

Remember: both give the SAME bonus when time saved is exactly 50% of time allowed. Below 50%, Rowan pays more; above 50%, Halsey pays more.
g2.link: Linked to today's case MCQ: Incentive plans – Rowan vs Halsey

g1.subject: GST – Sec 16(2)
g1.title: ITC conditions: 'I Received The Real Bill'
g1.body:
I – Invoice or debit note in hand
R – Received the goods or services
T – Tax actually paid to the Government by the supplier
R – Return (GSTR-3B) filed by you
B – Bill shown in your GSTR-2B

Plus: pay the supplier within 180 days of the invoice – otherwise the ITC is reversed (and can be taken again when you pay).
Prior payment is NOT a condition to claim ITC.
g1.link: Linked to today's general MCQ: Sec 16 – Input tax credit

g2.subject: Costing – Marginal costing
g2.title: BEP, Margin of Safety and Profit
g2.body:
BEP sales = Fixed cost ÷ P/V ratio
Margin of Safety = Actual sales − BEP sales
Profit = Margin of Safety × P/V ratio

Example: Sales ₹10 lakh, P/V ratio 40%, Fixed cost ₹2 lakh
BEP = 2 ÷ 40% = ₹5 lakh
MoS = 10 − 5 = ₹5 lakh
Profit = 5 × 40% = ₹2 lakh (check: contribution 4 − fixed 2 = 2 ✔️)

Common mistake: dividing fixed cost by the variable cost ratio.
g2.link: Linked to today's general MCQ: Marginal costing – BEP

g1.subject: GST – Sec 15
g1.title: Value of supply: what goes in, what stays out
g1.body:
Start with the transaction value (price actually paid, parties not related, price the sole consideration). Then ADD:
• Taxes, duties and fees other than GST
• Amounts the supplier owed but the buyer paid, if not already in the price
• Incidental expenses like packing and commission charged by the supplier
• Interest, late fee or penalty for delayed payment
• Subsidies directly linked to the price (except Government subsidies)

KEEP OUT:
• Discount given before or at the time of supply and shown on the invoice
• Post-supply discount – only if the conditions of Sec 15(3)(b) are met
g1.link: Linked to today's case MCQ: Value of outward supply

g2.subject: FM – Investment decisions
g2.title: ARR vs Payback period
g2.body:
ARR → uses ACCOUNTING PROFIT (after depreciation and tax). Payback → uses CASH FLOWS.

ARR = Average profit after tax ÷ Average (or initial) investment × 100. Payback = time taken to recover the initial investment.

ARR looks at profit over the WHOLE life. Payback ignores everything after the cost is recovered.

Both ignore the time value of money (use discounted payback, NPV or IRR for that).

Decision: ARR → accept if above the target rate. Payback → accept if shorter than the target period.
g2.link: Linked to today's case MCQ: Accounting Rate of Return

g1.subject: Income Tax – House property
g1.title: Self-occupied vs Let-out house
g1.body:
Annual value → Self-occupied: NIL. Let-out: Gross annual value (based on expected rent or actual rent, whichever is higher, with vacancy rules) less municipal taxes paid by the owner.

Standard deduction of 30% → Self-occupied: not available (annual value is nil). Let-out: 30% of net annual value.

Interest on housing loan → Self-occupied: allowed within a limit, and NOT under the default (new) tax regime. Let-out: allowed in full (loss set-off is limited).

Tip: always find the annual value first – the rest follows from it.
g1.link: Linked to today's general MCQ: House property – annual value

g2.subject: Costing – Employee cost
g2.title: Labour turnover: 3 methods
g2.body:
Separation method = Separations ÷ Average workers × 100
Replacement method = Replacements ÷ Average workers × 100
Flux method = (Separations + Replacements) ÷ Average workers × 100

Example: Average 500, separations 20, replacements 15
Separation = 4%, Replacement = 3%, Flux = 7%

If there are new joinings for expansion, flux can also be shown as (Separations + Accessions) ÷ Average × 100, where accessions = replacements + new joinings.
Always use the AVERAGE number of workers: (opening + closing) ÷ 2.
g2.link: Linked to today's general MCQ: Labour turnover

g1.subject: Law – LLP Act, Sec 7
g1.title: Designated partners
g1.body:
• Every LLP must have at least 2 designated partners, who are individuals.
• At least one of them must be resident in India.
• Resident in India: stayed in India for at least 120 days during the financial year.
• If all partners are bodies corporate, their nominees act as designated partners.
• A designated partner needs a DPIN / DIN and must give prior consent.
• Designated partners are responsible for compliance with the Act and are liable to penalties for default.
g1.link: Linked to today's case MCQ: LLP Act – Resident designated partner

g2.subject: Costing – Process costing
g2.title: Normal loss, abnormal loss, abnormal gain
g2.body:
• Normal loss: expected → its cost is absorbed by good units; scrap value credited to the process.
• Abnormal loss: more than normal → valued like good units, transferred to Abnormal Loss A/c → Costing P&L.
• Abnormal gain: actual loss less than normal → valued like good units, debited to the process; credited to Abnormal Gain A/c.
• Abnormal gain also reduces the scrap that was expected from normal loss – adjust this in the Abnormal Gain A/c.
• Cost per unit = (Total cost − scrap value of normal loss) ÷ (Input − normal loss units).
g2.link: Linked to today's case MCQ: Process costing – abnormal gain

g1.subject: Income Tax – Clubbing
g1.title: Gift to wife – whose income?
g1.body:
❌ Mr. A gifts ₹10 lakh to his wife. She puts it in a fixed deposit, and the interest is shown in HER return.

✅ Correct: transfer of an asset to the spouse without adequate consideration → the income from it is CLUBBED with Mr. A's income.

Also remember:
• Minor child's income → clubbed with the parent having higher income (not if from the child's own skill or manual work).
• Income earned on the clubbed income (second-level income) is NOT clubbed – it is the wife's own income.
g1.link: Linked to today's general MCQ: Clubbing of income

g2.subject: FM – Dividend decision
g2.title: Walter's model
g2.body:
P = [D + (r ÷ k) × (E − D)] ÷ k
P = price per share, D = dividend, E = EPS, r = return on investment, k = cost of equity

Example: E ₹10, D ₹4, r 15%, k 10%
P = [4 + 1.5 × 6] ÷ 0.10 = ₹130
With 0% payout: P = [0 + 1.5 × 10] ÷ 0.10 = ₹150

Rule: r > k → retain all (0% payout). r < k → pay all (100%). r = k → payout does not matter.
g2.link: Linked to today's general MCQ: Walter's model

g1.subject: Law – Sec 103 & 105
g1.title: Quorum and proxy
g1.body:
Quorum (members personally present) – public company:
• Up to 1,000 members → 5
• 1,000 to 5,000 members → 15
• More than 5,000 members → 30
Private company → 2 (unless the articles say more).

Proxy:
• A member can appoint a proxy, who need not be a member.
• A proxy cannot speak and votes only on a poll.
• Proxy form must reach the company at least 48 hours before the meeting.
• One person can be proxy for at most 50 members holding up to 10% of the voting share capital.
g1.link: Linked to today's case MCQ: Sec 103 & 105 – Quorum and proxy

g2.subject: Audit – SA 315
g2.title: Assertions made easy
g2.body:
Account balances at year-end – 'Every Rupee Counts, Verify':
E – Existence
R – Rights and obligations
C – Completeness
V – Valuation and allocation

Transactions during the year – 'Only Clever Auditors Check Carefully':
O – Occurrence
C – Completeness
A – Accuracy
C – Cut-off
C – Classification

Plus presentation and disclosure. Tip: existence → test from records to the asset; completeness → test from the source to the records.
g2.link: Linked to today's case MCQ: Assertions
